title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a long hymn to the goddess opens with a sentence about a god who cannot even stir

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's snake: coiled or gliding, one snake, the way one reality rests or works. Today, one verse puts it in Shiva's terms.

A long Sanskrit hymn to the goddess, the Saundarya Lahari, the wave of beauty, opens in a strange place. Not with her face, her weapons or her lion. It begins with Shiva, the great god of the mountain, the destroyer, the lord of yogis. And what stands out in that first verse is what he can't do. Without her, the verse says, he can't create. He can't even stir. Tradition says the hymn comes from Shankara, the teacher of non-duality. Whoever wrote it chose to open a praise of the goddess with God standing perfectly still.
screen: `THE WAVE OF BEAUTY.` → `IT OPENS WITH SHIVA.` → `WITHOUT HER, HE CAN'T STIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Shiva, joined with Shakti, is able to create. If not, this god is not even able to move. So how could anyone without merit bow to you, or praise you, you who are worshipped by Vishnu, by Shiva, by Brahma? First, the play on words in the Sanskrit. Joined with shakti, power, the word this path first met in Durga's story, Shiva becomes shakta, able. The verse sets the two sounds side by side, and the second time the sound means capable. Second, the couple. In the Puranas, Shiva and Parvati are married, with children. The verse doesn't deny that. But it says something sharper. She isn't only his wife. She is the reason anything he does gets done. Stillness on one side, movement on the other, and nothing happens until the two are together. Third, the ending. Vishnu who protects, Brahma who creates, Shiva who dissolves: in this hymn, all of them stand before her. Some who worship the goddess hear that line as the whole point. In their reading, power isn't a tool God picks up. It's the face of God that acts. And a fourth, smaller way in. Some readers carry the verse home into ordinary life. A plan with no energy behind it sits on the table; a good intention that never moves is still just an intention. Stillness and power: the one who knows, and the force that does.
screen: `JOINED WITH SHAKTI, SHIVA IS ABLE.` · `SHAKTI AND SHAKTA: POWER AND ABLE.` · `NOT ONLY HIS WIFE: HIS POWER TO ACT.` · `THE GODS THEMSELVES BOW TO HER.` · then, large: `WITHOUT HER, HE CANNOT EVEN STIR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been meaning to start, sitting still like a plan on the table. On each in-breath, picture its very first small step; on each out-breath, let the picture rest, the way the verse joins stillness and stir. If you pray, you can hold the name Shakti, or Devi, or Ma, with each breath out. If you don't, let the breath carry the plan.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the wave of beauty's opening verse, Shiva joined with Shakti is able to create. Without her, he cannot even stir.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. A god at rest, and the power that lets him move. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Saundarya Lahari is chanted and studied by worshippers of the goddess, including in the Shri Vidya tradition, and a reading of it begins with this verse.

chat.says: Why would a hymn to the goddess start with Shiva unable to move?
options: To show his power to act is her: joined with Shakti he creates; without her, he can't stir.
Because Shiva is resting after a long battle, and the hymn waits for him to wake.
Because the verse says she can only act once Shiva gives her permission to move.
chat.meaning: In the Saundarya Lahari's first verse, Shiva joined with Shakti can create; without her he can't even stir. She is the power that acts.
